title: The Red Alert
mood: A red message, a pull in every cell, and a trade Selena is sure she controls.

hero.alt: On a bright morning Selena, a blonde student in uniform with small red horns, kicks one foot up on a ledge by a railing, past a no-climbing sign and a CAUTION sign, her silver dragon machine Silverbolt crackling with blue light beside her.

segs.t: Selena sat in the front row with her pen on a half-written line. At the screen the teacher was going down a table: this year’s suits, each kind and each rank, and how strong each could run.
Her phone lit red by her elbow, with no name and no words.
The pull came with it from over the bay. Every cell in her body strained toward it at once, harder than ever before.
Her pen stopped.
Nobody turned.
Not here,
she thought.
The first alert had come on a cold, bright morning. That day she had kept drawing.
The end of the year before.
“Up. You’ll be late.”
Karina stood in the bedroom door at dawn, boots laced, her rescue helmet under her arm.
“I’m coming already! Geez, what’s the rush?” Selena pulled the blanket over her head.
“The bell,” said Karina. She took the blanket with her when she went.
Silverbolt waited at the foot of Karina’s stair. Out on the street Selena pinned on her horned headband and let her own two horns up through her hair. Then she rode to school.
The road ran between fences hung with signs: NO CROSSING, CAUTION. Silverbolt’s claws clicked on the cold stones.
At the metal fence with the NEXT STOP sign, her phone buzzed against her hip.
Between a workshop’s order and a classmate’s nagging sat one more message, from nobody: a red exclamation mark, and nothing else.
Then something tugged at every cell in her at once, from somewhere far past the sky. It did not hurt. Her body knew what it meant before she did.
Come back.
All her life Enders had hummed in her bones. This was the hum with a hook in it.
“Ugh, what a horrible feeling.” Selena glared at the fence.
Years of nothing,
she thought.
And now this.
Since the showing, half the Academy knew her name.
Maybe I’ve been too good.
She swiped the message off the screen. The pull stayed.

So she rode slower. At the Academy steps she slid off Silverbolt on purpose, landed on her toes and skipped down the classroom hallway with the machine clicking beside her. Whoever was in a hurry could wait.
The hall doors stood open. Students poured out of a ceremony, cheering. In the crowd a pink-haired girl held a new badge over her head.
Selena had missed it. She slipped into the next lesson on foot, Silverbolt at her heel.
Chang’e sat on her stool by the screen. At the back sat two girls with new badges still pinned on, one pink-haired, one black-haired.
Selena opened her sketch. Line by line, the armor went on growing.
“We think it is a mind,” Chang’e was saying. “The Will of the Planet.” It had a body too, the readings suggested. “We call that the Mother Matrix.”
Mother Matrix.
Her cells knew what it named. She had never heard the name before.
Her pen kept moving. A shoulder plate. A joint that bent the wrong way for a human.
Chang’e spoke of a dark called the void. “Nobody can get near it.”
It got near me fine this morning,
thought Selena.
At a bus stop.
The bright day clouded over at dusk. After dark a storm came in off the bay.
Selena climbed out onto the bell tower’s tiles with Silverbolt behind her. Thunder had always put her bones at rest.
Tonight the pull came down with the rain, and her phone lit red again in her pocket.

Selena deliberately ignored the mysterious transmission buried among her messages. She knew exactly what it was: a recall from the Enders, a command etched deep into her cells, and an invisible shackle trying to drag her back to the cold, rigid Mother Matrix.
Not once,
she thought.
Not ever.
She swung onto Silverbolt’s back and took it off the tower and out over the outskirts. She shed her jacket and let the purple out.
They ran, roof to roof. The pull did not fall behind. On every roof it sat in her cells, exactly as strong.
At the edge of a gap, Silverbolt stopped.
It stood in the rain with its claws hooked over the ledge. Its motor dropped to a hum. Then it lifted its head, slowly, and turned it up toward the sky.
Selena’s hands went still on its plates.
It moved when she meant it to. Before her hands did. So some part of her meant this.
Her own cells were pulling the same way, up into the rain.
“Not you too,” she said. “Go.”
Silverbolt stood the way it had stood for Chang’e.
“Go.”
It went, and cleared the gap. On the far ledge its claws slid once on the wet stone, then held.
On her first run she had laughed on a roof like this one. She had thought,
Nobody can call me back.
Somebody can,
she thought now.
Through my own machine.
She rode until the storm blew itself out. The pull did not go with it.
She did not sleep that night, or the next. On the third morning a line on the armor came out crooked, the first in the whole drawing. Selena looked at it for a long time.
I can’t cut it,
she thought.
I can’t outrun it. Everything else in this city has a price. Fine. So does this.
The next storm, on the broken wall where she had sat after her first run, she laid both hands on Silverbolt’s back and let the purple into its core.
The pull ran through her, through the Ender plates she had bolted on, and up into the dark.
It’s a line,
she thought.
Lines run both ways.
She pushed, carefully, the way she woke a core. Something gave. Beside the pull a thin thread opened, hers alone. It went up into the dark and told her nothing of where it ended.
She had watched Chang’e’s screens pick up every Ender signal near the dome. In clear weather a signal sent like this would spike on them. In a storm, the lightning buried it.
Selena plugged her phone into the socket under the seat and began to write.
“Not coming back,” she said as she typed it at the top. “Let’s trade.”

Under it went the Academy’s routines, the dull ones: when the bells rang, when exams came. Last year’s suit specifications. How aspirant power drove a suit. How strong a suit could run, by kind and by rank.
She typed one more line, the hour the shore ward changed its watch, and deleted it. No name went in at all. Not the two girls with the new badges, not anyone.
Never a name,
she thought.
Never a place where people die.
The rest was stale, she told herself. Anyone who had fought a suit knew how it moved.
She sent it. Blue light ran up Silverbolt’s seams to its head and went out.
“Control me, break me, I don’t care. Because in the end, I’m always the one pulling the strings.” Selena said it with her face tipped up into the rain.
Thunder rolled over the bay. Nothing answered.
The answer took its time.
For a week the pull sank to a murmur. She slept. She rubbed out the crooked line and drew it again, straight.
Then one morning at the sink a place came into her head: a ditch out in the dead ground, past the crews’ yard, and a downed Ender lying in it. She had never been there. She knew it anyway.
She went out on her salvage pass before the crews were up. It lay where her head had said. She stripped it by noon and sold the plates that night for twice the crews’ price.
Not a leash,
she thought, counting.
A market.
The market ran the other way too. Before a raid she felt the Enders’ hum gather in her bones, a day early. A day was worth money. Her comms were never quiet.
A merchant on the waterfront paid her for one word.
“When?” he asked.
“Tomorrow.”
He moved his stock out of his warehouse that afternoon. The next night its roof came in.

One storm night on the wall she laid out in her head everything she had sold. Put together, it showed every suit in the Academy from the inside. With enough pieces like that, somebody could build a weapon against every one of them.
If anyone ever points it at the Academy,
she thought,
I’ll break it myself.
She did not ask herself why she would bother.
In the classroom the phone was still red.
Selena thumbed the message away. The pull stayed. She finished her line.
“Selena,” said the teacher. “The top row, please.”
She put the polite smile back on and read it out. Every number in it was higher than the ones she had sold.
Stale,
she told herself, and turned the phone face down on the desk.
